story_text.value:
I'm Dustin Kirkland, author of Byobu. I recently flew to Australia and kept nudging my Claude, Codex, and Bash jobs along back home from somewhere over the Pacific, at 700ms of latency.

That's what Trustmux is for: secure, asynchronous access to your tmux or Byobu sessions from your phone.

I first posted this in June and since then there have been many point releases, lots of new features and testing, and a growing base of users. It's now packaged in Ubuntu 26.10, Debian, Fedora, and Chainguard OS.

Why not SSH, Mosh, or Claude Mobile?

- SSH/Mosh: a live, synchronous connection is brutal on a phone. Latency and WiFi-to-cellular handoffs make it laggy and fragile. - Claude Mobile: great for Claude, but I wanted access to whatever is running in my tmux session: shells, Claude, other code assistants.

Trustmux is async by design. Connect, look, type a command, disconnect, with no fragile connection state to babysit.

Security: TLS with real certificates, end to end. Uses Tailscale (cert provisioning via tailscale serve, no port forwarding) optionally, bind to your own network address, or bring your own or self-signed certs. Two security experts reviewed the design and I implemented their recommendations. More scrutiny is very welcome.

Quick start:

  trustmux enable
  trustmux start
  trustmux pair   # shows a QR code if qrencode is installed
Open the URL on your phone, enter the 6-digit code, and add it to your home screen. It's a PWA, so there's no app store.

Install: apt, dnf, pip install trustmux, or brew tap dustinkirkland/trustmux && brew install trustmux

Under the hood: Python, libtmux, WebSockets, Tailscale, and no polling. The UI shell is cached for offline use. Part of Byobu, GPLv3. Trustmux isn't affiliated with the tmux project.

https://trustmux.dev https://github.com/dustinkirkland/byobu https://pypi.org/project/trustmux/

story_text.value:
Hi HN Folks,

I have been building Kitaphone a web app that lets you call regular mobile and landline numbers directly from your browser. The idea is simple, there are still plenty of situations where apps like WhatsApp, facetime and other internet calling apps aren't an option. For example, when you are abroad and need to call your bank, an airline, or a government office or your son/daughter's school.

I wanted to make those calls possible without requiring users to install another app or buy a sim card or even commit to a monthly subscription. I built Kitaphone using Next.js and Twilio, One of the more interesting challenges has been making browser based calling reliable, especially when it comes to dealing with microphone permissions, sending keypad inputs to automated phone systems, and preventing abuse of free calling credits.

The product is live and supports international calls to regular phone numbers, users currently need an account to make calls partly because each call has a real telecom cost. I am still improving it and learning from the people using it by receiving feedback.

Fun fact: "kita" means our in Bahasa Malaysia, since I am based in this beautiful country and their people are so warm and welcoming I was truly inspired by this place and decided to name it our phone.

Interested to know or receive feedback from HN folks who worked with WebRTC or VoiP in the past.

story_text.value:
Shipped Beeline today. It's a team chat for humans and agents - a kind of multiplayer harness. You can bring your codex, Claude code, opencode subscriptions and also works with pi and goose. We built beeline itself with early versions of beeline, and use it to build our other projects - it's boosted productivity quite a bit for us.

Demo video: https://youtu.be/ACdelpZC2z4?is=pP6MFxJODvKcGjQt

The key insight is that humans do their best work in teams, but agentic development has so far been single player. This has led to people having to forward AI slop to each other or to try to deliver context through various shims like meetings or task tickets.

Beeline is a single control plane for your entire team, both human and agent, and is designed to help your team do its best work.

Things to expect: - This is a multiplayer agentic harness, not a slack substitute. It's best for focused product teams doing or relying on engineering tools and shipping code. - Open source and not a business. We use beeline internally, and just thought it would be a really cool thing to exist in the world. There are still lots of bugs - Sweepstakes things like computer use, lots of third party connector integrations are there. What's cool is that beeline agents can automate _auth_ through trustysquire.ai - they can sign up to most services and APIs without you having to do it for them. - A new primitive called workflows, that are skills for teams of agents. - multi way call with your entire team, humans and agents. I like it quite a bit.

Looking forward to feedback!

title.value: Show HN: Beeline Multiplayer Agent Harness

story_text.value:
As an IT professional, I felt a distinct lacking of a real-time tool for tracking down problems in complex systems. I have created Wayseer Desktop as a way to explore more effective ways to explore live systems.

There's a very functional free version, and paid options that unlock additional features. I'm curious what you all think of the approach. I'm a systems engineer by trade (with some development experience), not a developer, so I have relied on AI to do the heavy lifting while I request features, report bugs and perform as much manual testing as I feasibly can.

There are bound to be bugs... but it is still very young and has a (hopefully) long future in which refinements can be made.

story_text.value:
I built this for myself. I often have questions I want quick answers to such as "how cold did it get last night?", "I just put down fertilizer, when will it rain next?", "is today unusually cold or warm for this time of year?" Weather sites I tried made me dig for those answers, if they were there at all (the last few days of weather often can't be found).

I used to watch a few stocks closely, and Weatheristic is actually inspired by those types of charts. It has day/night bands with an ultra easy to understand temp trend line, and you can zoom and scroll. I added data I'm interested in, such as a typical high/low band, record high/low for today, moon phases, and various other items in the Overlays dropdown.

One deliberate choice: the temperature scale doesn’t rescale. It stays at roughly -4F to 86F (−20C to 30C) most of the time, so the line’s height on the y-axis tells you how warm it is before you read a number. So if the graph seems off center to you, that's by design.

Data comes from Open-Meteo. The historical records come from their reanalysis archive, which is modelled data rather than weather-station readings, so daily extremes might be a bit off. It’s a static D3 site. No account, no ads, no cookies. I count visits with self-hosted Plausible (cookieless, no personal data; it lives at analytics.povodex.com because I run it for my other projects too).

I use this every day, love it, and I’d love to know if anyone else likes this format.

title.value: Show HN: Weatheristic.com to answer questions other weather sites don't
